concepts.title: Classes, Objects, and Encapsulation
concepts.description: A class is a blueprint bundling state (fields) and behavior (methods); objects are the instances built from it via constructors. Encapsulation keeps fields private behind chosen methods, so a class can enforce rules about its own state.
learningObjectives: Define a class with instance fields, one or more constructors, and instance methods, and explain precisely what new does when an object is created.
Explain what this refers to inside a constructor or instance method, and when it's required to disambiguate a field from a same-named parameter.
Use constructor overloading and constructor chaining with this(...) to avoid duplicating initialization logic across constructors.
Explain why fields are conventionally declared private and exposed only through deliberately-written methods, in terms of invariants the class can guarantee.
Explain why returning a direct reference to a mutable field (like a list or array) from a getter breaks encapsulation even though the field itself is private.
Predict an object's field values after a sequence of constructor calls and mutating method calls.

sections.heading: Classes as Blueprints, Objects as Instances
Constructors: Controlling How an Object Comes Into Existence
Encapsulation: Why Fields Are private
sections.body:
**Encapsulation** means bundling an object's state together with the code that's allowed to touch it, and restricting outside access to that state so it can only be read or changed through methods the class itself provides. The conventional Java idiom is: fields are `private`, and any access from outside the class goes through public methods: getters to read, setters (or more specific, purpose-built methods) to write.

The reason is what the class can *guarantee*. A `private double balance` with no public setter, only a `deposit(double amount)` method that rejects negative amounts, can genuinely promise that `balance` never goes negative through any code outside the class: every path that could change it is one the class itself controls and can validate. A `public double balance` field offers no such guarantee at all: any code anywhere that has a reference to the object can write `account.balance = -500;`, bypassing every rule the class might have wanted to enforce, because there's no method in the way to enforce anything. A rule that should always hold about an object's state is called an **invariant**, and a class can only defend one if it controls every write.

Encapsulation also lets you *change* a class's internal representation later without breaking code that uses it. If `balance` is private and only ever read through `getBalance()`, you're free to later change how the balance is actually stored internally (as a `long` count of cents, say, since `double` can't represent 0.10 exactly and is a poor choice for money) without touching a single line of calling code, as long as `getBalance()` still returns a `double` matching the old contract. With a public field, changing its type or name breaks every caller.

sections.heading: The Leaky Getter Trap

examples.title: Two Independent Objects From One Class
examples.explanation: `new Counter(0)` and `new Counter(100)` each allocate a fresh object on the heap with their own, independent `count` field. There is no shared storage between `a` and `b` at all, even though they were built from identical code. Calling `a.increment()` twice mutates only `a`'s own `count`, taking it from 0 to 2; it has zero effect on `b`'s count, which starts from a completely different value (100) and is only ever incremented by the one call `b.increment()` makes on it, landing at 101. Inside `increment()`, the bare name `count` means `this.count`, and `this` is whichever object the method was called on.

examples.title: Constructor Chaining Avoids Duplicated Validation Logic
examples.explanation: The one-argument constructor doesn't repeat the validation or the field assignments at all; `this(side, side)` delegates straight to the two-argument constructor, passing `side` for both width and height, and that constructor's validation and assignment logic runs exactly as it would for any other caller. Because `this(...)` must be the first statement in a constructor, there's no way to accidentally skip past the validation on this path; every route to constructing a `Rectangle`, however many convenience constructors are added later, funnels through that single two-argument constructor's checks. Calling `new Rectangle(-2.0)` proves this: even though the caller only ever touched the *one*-argument constructor, the exception thrown by the validation inside the two-argument constructor still fires, because chaining runs that constructor's body.

examples.title: Fixing a Leaky Getter With a Defensive Copy
examples.explanation: `getMembers()` now returns `new ArrayList<>(members)`, a brand-new list object populated with the same elements, not the original `members` list itself. Calling `snapshot.add("Zoe")` mutates that new, independent list; it has no path back to the actual `members` field living inside `team`, so the team's roster is completely unaffected. The only sanctioned way to change `team`'s roster is `addMember(...)`, which is as it should be the point: the class gets to decide what 'adding a member' means (validation, deduplication, logging, whatever it needs) because there's now no other way in.

misconceptions.description: Declaring a field private is sufficient, on its own, to fully protect an object's internal state from outside mutation.
misconceptions.clarification: private stops outside code from accessing the field *by name* (`obj.field`), but it does nothing to protect the object that field refers to, if that object is mutable and a method hands out a direct reference to it. A getter that does `return someMutableField;` gives the caller a live, working reference to the exact same object. Callers can then call mutating methods on it (`.add()`, `.set()`, `.clear()`) and change the class's internal state with the class never knowing. To protect a mutable field, return a defensive copy or a read-only view such as Collections.unmodifiableList(field).
misconceptions.fact: private stops outside code from accessing the field *by name* (`obj.field`), but it does nothing to protect the object that field refers to, if that object is mutable and a method hands out a direct reference to it.

misconceptions.description: Every class automatically gets a no-argument constructor from Java, regardless of what other constructors you've written.
misconceptions.clarification: Java only supplies the automatic, do-nothing default constructor when a class defines *no* constructors of its own at all. The instant you write even one constructor (with any parameter list) that automatic default disappears completely; if you still want callers to be able to write `new MyClass()` with no arguments, you must write that zero-argument constructor yourself, explicitly. This is a common source of a specific compile error (something like `constructor MyClass in class MyClass cannot be applied to given types`) for someone who added a parameterized constructor and then, elsewhere in the code, tried to call the no-argument form they assumed would still be there.
misconceptions.fact: Java only supplies the automatic, do-nothing default constructor when a class defines *no* constructors of its own at all.

exercises.prompt: What does this program print, and why?
hints: Wallet is a class, so a and b are reference variables. What does `Wallet b = a;` copy: the object, or the reference to it?
Since b and a end up pointing at the same object, does calling deposit through b affect what a sees when it reads balance afterward?
c is created independently with `new Wallet(50.0)`: it has never had any connection to a or b at all.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 75.0, then 75.0. a and b refer to the same Wallet object, so b.deposit(25.0) is visible through a too, giving 75.0. c is a completely separate object that also had 25.0 deposited into it, independently arriving at 75.0 as well, but for an unrelated reason.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `Wallet b = a;` copies the reference stored in `a` into `b`, like the array-aliasing behavior from earlier in the course, this does not create a second Wallet object; a and b are now two names for the one and only object created by `new Wallet(50.0)`. Calling `b.deposit(25.0)` mutates that single shared object's balance field from 50.0 to 75.0, and since a points at that same object, `a.getBalance()` correctly reports 75.0 too. `c`, by contrast, is a separate object created by its own `new Wallet(50.0)` call, with its own independent balance field; depositing 25.0 into it also brings it to 75.0, but this is a coincidence of using the same numbers, not any shared state. C was never aliased to a or b at any point.

exercises.prompt: This class is meant to guarantee that an Employee's salary is never set to a negative number, but the bug below shows that guarantee doesn't actually hold. Find and fix the bug.
hints: The constructor's validation only runs once, when the object is first created. Is there any OTHER way, besides the constructor, that code outside the class can change salary?
Look at how salary is declared: is it private, the way name is?
Making the field private removes the direct-assignment path; you'll then need a method (a setter) that re-runs the same validation for any later changes.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The constructor's validation only ever runs at construction time. It says nothing about what happens afterward, and `salary` was declared `public`, which means any code anywhere with a reference to an Employee could write `e.salary = -1000.0;`, completely bypassing the constructor and its check. The fix has two parts: make `salary` `private`, which removes the direct-assignment path (that line would now fail to compile from outside the class), and add a `setSalary` method that re-runs the same validation before changing the field, giving the class a controlled, single path for changing salary after construction. To avoid two copies of the check drifting apart, the constructor could call a private validation method that setSalary shares.

assessments.prompt: A class has a private field `private List<String> items;` and a getter `public List<String> getItems() { return items; }`. What is the problem with this getter, if any?
options: There is no problem -- private fields are always fully protected regardless of what a getter returns.
The getter returns a direct reference to the actual internal list.
This code fails to compile, because a getter cannot return a reference type.
The problem is that getItems() should be named differently, since 'get' should only be used for primitive fields.
assessments.explanation: Returning `items` hands the caller the exact same List object the class holds internally. Since lists are mutable, the caller can call mutating methods on that reference and change the class's internal state, with the class having no say in it and no way to validate the change. The “There is no problem -- private fields…” option is wrong because private only blocks direct field access by name, not mutation through a returned reference to a mutable object. The “This code fails to compile…” option is wrong: returning a reference type from a getter is completely ordinary and legal. The “The problem is that getItems() should…” option is a fabricated, irrelevant naming rule.

assessments.prompt: Explain what encapsulation actually buys a class, using the idea of invariants, and explain why a private field with a getter that leaks a mutable reference only looks like encapsulation.
assessments.modelAnswer: Encapsulation means bundling an object's state with the code permitted to touch it, and routing every outside interaction with that state through methods the class itself writes and controls, typically by making fields private and exposing only-chosen public methods. The payoff is that the class can guarantee its invariants: rules about its own state that should always hold true, like a bank balance never going negative or a list never containing duplicate entries. If every path that can change that state is a method the class wrote, the class can put a check at the top of that method and know that the check runs on every call, because there is no other way in. A public field offers no such guarantee: any code anywhere holding a reference to the object can assign to that field, bypassing every rule the class might want to enforce, since there's no method standing in the way to enforce anything. The subtler failure mode is a field that's private, with no public setter, but a getter that returns the internal object when that object happens to be mutable (an ArrayList, say, rather than an int. This looks encapsulated from the outside: there's no way to write `obj.field = ...`. But the caller who receives that returned list can call .add() or .remove() or .clear() on it, and because it's the exact same object the class holds internally (not a copy) those mutations land on the class's internal state, with the class having no idea it happened and no chance to validate or reject it. The fix is a defensive copy: return a new collection built from the internal one, so callers can look at (or even freely mutate their own copy of) the data without any of it reaching back into the object's internals.

assessments.prompt: class Point { private int x; private int y; public Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } } Point p = new Point(); What happens?
options: This compiles fine and creates a Point with x and y both defaulting to 0.
This throws a NullPointerException at run time, since x and y are never initialized.

This compiles fine, since Java always provides a no-argument constructor for every class, regardless of what else is declared, so p is created with x and y both set to zero and the two-argument constructor remains available too.

This fails to compile, because the moment a class defines any constructor of its own, the automatic no-argument default constructor disappears entirely -- Point has no accessible zero-argument constructor for new Point() to call.
assessments.explanation: Java only supplies the automatic, do-nothing default constructor when a class defines no constructors at all. Point defines one constructor, taking (int, int), so that automatic default is gone; there is no zero-argument constructor available for new Point() to invoke, and the compiler rejects the call rather than inventing one. The “This compiles fine, since Java always provides…” option describes behavior that only holds for classes with no constructors written at all. The “This compiles fine and creates a Point…” option assumes a default constructor exists when it does not. The “This throws a NullPointerException at run time…” option is wrong because this code never reaches run time in the first place; the failure is caught by javac before any object could ever be created.

assessments.prompt: class Person { private String name; public Person(String name) { name = name; } public String getName() { return name; } } What does new Person("Amy").getName() return, and why?
options: null, because the bare name on the left of name = name refers to the parameter, which shadows the field inside the constructor -- the assignment sets the parameter to itself, and the field name never receives the argument at all, keeping its default value.
"Amy", because name = name correctly assigns the constructor parameter's value into the field.
This fails to compile, because Java forbids assigning a variable to itself.
"", because uninitialized String fields default to an empty string rather than null.
assessments.explanation: Inside the constructor, the parameter name shadows the field of the same name; a bare name refers to the parameter, not this.name, unless this. is written explicitly. name = name is therefore a self-assignment of the parameter to itself; it never touches the field. Since String fields default to null when never assigned, getName() returns null, not "Amy". It compiles and throws nothing, so you only notice when the name turns up null. The “"Amy", because name = name correctly assigns…” option assumes the bare name resolves to the field, which is the shadowing mistake. The “This fails to compile, because Java forbids…” option is wrong because self-assignment is completely legal Java. The “"", because uninitialized String fields default…” option is wrong about String's default value, which is null, not an empty string.

assessments.prompt: public class Rectangle { private double width, height; public Rectangle(double width, double height) { if (width <= 0 || height <= 0) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid"); } this.width = width; this.height = height; } public Rectangle(double side) { System.out.println("creating square"); this(side, side); } } What is wrong with the second constructor in Java 21?
options: This fails to compile, because a constructor is never allowed to call another constructor of the same class under any circumstance, with or without a println.
Nothing -- this compiles and works exactly as intended.
This fails to compile, because a call to this(...) must be the very first statement in a constructor, and here it's preceded by a println statement.
This compiles fine but silently skips the validation logic in the two-argument constructor.
assessments.explanation: In Java 21 a this(...) call must be the first statement in the constructor body, so the println before it is a compile error. (Java 25 relaxed the rule and would accept this constructor.) The “Nothing -- this compiles and works exactly as intended” option is wrong because Java 21 enforces the ordering. The “This fails to compile, because a constructor…” option is wrong because calling another constructor with this(...) is legal as long as it comes first. The “This compiles fine but silently skips…” option is wrong because the code doesn't compile, and chaining would run the validation if it did.

concepts.title: Inheritance: extends and super
concepts.description: Inheritance lets one class (a subclass) acquire the fields and methods of another (a superclass) via extends, and override methods to specialize behavior. super lets a subclass call its superclass's constructor or the superclass version of an overridden method.
learningObjectives: Define a subclass with extends and explain what it inherits automatically from its superclass, and what it does not (private members, constructors).
Override an inherited method correctly using @Override, and explain how the actual (run-time) type of an object -- not the declared type of the reference -- determines which overridden version runs.
Explain why a subclass constructor must invoke a superclass constructor, implicitly or explicitly via super(...), as its very first action.
Use super.methodName() to call an overridden superclass method from inside the overriding subclass method, and explain when this is necessary.
Distinguish overriding from overloading, and predict compile errors caused by an invalid @Override.
Trace the exact order of constructor calls up an inheritance chain when a subclass object is created.

sections.heading: extends: What a Subclass Inherits
Constructors and super(...)
Overriding: Same Signature, New Body, Chosen at Run Time
super.method(): Reaching Back to the Overridden Version

examples.title: Constructor Chaining Order Up an Inheritance Hierarchy
examples.explanation: Even though none of these constructors writes a `super()` call, Java inserts `super()` as the first statement of every constructor that doesn't call one explicitly. So `Puppy()`'s implicit first action is calling `Dog()`'s constructor, whose own implicit first action is calling `Animal()`'s constructor, whose implicit first action calls `Object`'s (built-in, does nothing observable here). Execution therefore runs top-down from the top of the hierarchy: `Animal`'s body finishes first (printing 'Animal constructor'), then control returns to `Dog`'s body, which finishes next ('Dog constructor'), and only then does `Puppy`'s own body finally run ('Puppy constructor'). One consequence to watch for: if `Animal`'s constructor calls a method that `Puppy` overrides, `Puppy`'s version runs before `Puppy`'s own fields are set. Avoid calling overridable methods from constructors.

examples.title: Overriding Is Resolved by Run-Time Type, Not Declared Type
examples.explanation: Every element of the `shapes` array is *declared* as `Shape`, but each one's ** object is a `Circle` or a `Square`, and `s.area()` dispatches based on that run-time, run-time type every single time through the loop. The exact same line of code, `s.area()`, runs a completely different method body depending on which object `s` currently refers to. Code written once against `Shape` runs each subclass's own behavior without an if/else or switch checking 'is this a Circle or a Square' anywhere. `Shape` itself never needs to know how many kinds of shapes will eventually exist: any new subclass that overrides `area()` correctly would work in this same loop with zero changes to the loop itself.

examples.title: super.method() Extends Behavior Instead of Duplicating It
examples.explanation: `Manager.calculatePay()` doesn't reimplement the base salary logic at all. `super.calculatePay()` calls Employee's own version, which returns `baseSalary` (80000.0), and Manager's override adds `bonus` (15000.0) on top of that, giving 95000.0. If Employee's pay calculation later grew more complex (say, factoring in years of service), Manager's override would automatically pick up that change through `super.calculatePay()`, with zero edits needed in Manager itself. Contrast this with what would happen if Manager's override called `this.calculatePay()` instead of `super.calculatePay()`: since `this` always dispatches to the run-time type's version, and the run-time type here is Manager, `this.calculatePay()` would call Manager's own override again, which would call itself again, and so on, an infinite recursion ending in a StackOverflowError, not the intended behavior at all.

misconceptions.description: A subclass automatically inherits its superclass's constructors, the same way it inherits methods.
misconceptions.clarification: Constructors are excluded from what extends hands down. A subclass must define its own constructors, and every one of them must invoke some constructor of the superclass (implicitly (an inserted, no-argument super()) or explicitly (a super(...) call you write yourself)) as its first action. The superclass's fields have to be set up by its own constructor before subclass code relies on them.

misconceptions.description: Calling an overridden method through a variable declared as the superclass type runs the superclass's version of that method, since that's the declared type.
misconceptions.clarification: Overriding is resolved by the object's actual, run-time type, completely independent of how the reference variable holding it happens to be declared. `Animal a = new Dog();` followed by `a.makeSound();` runs Dog's overriding version, not Animal's. The declared type `Animal` only constrains which methods and fields you're allowed to reference through `a` at compile time (you couldn't call a Dog-only method through an Animal-typed reference without a cast), it does not determine which overridden method body executes. That dispatch decision is made at run time, based on the object, which is why this mechanism is called run-time polymorphism.
misconceptions.fact: Overriding is resolved by the object's actual, run-time type, completely independent of how the reference variable holding it happens to be declared.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and why?
hints: Constructing a Car always runs Vehicle's constructor first, whether or not super() is written: track the print order across both constructors.
v is declared as Vehicle, but the object is a Car: which describe() runs when v.describe() is called?
Inside Car's describe(), super.describe() calls Vehicle's own version, not Car's: trace what string that produces and how Car's override builds on top of it.
exercises.expectedAnswer:
Vehicle created
Car created
a car, which is a vehicle. Construction prints top-down (superclass first), and describe() dispatches to Car's override based on the run-time type, which itself calls super.describe() to build on Vehicle's text.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Constructing `new Car()` first runs Vehicle's constructor (via the super() call, which must be the first statement), printing 'Vehicle created', and only then does Car's own constructor body run, printing 'Car created'. After construction, v.describe() is called through a reference declared as Vehicle, but the object is a Car, and overriding dispatches based on that type, so Car's override runs. Inside it, super.describe() calls Vehicle's version, returning 'a vehicle', and Car's override appends that into 'a car, which is a vehicle', which is what ultimately gets printed.

exercises.prompt: This code is meant to have Square override Rectangle's area() calculation, but it fails to compile, for two separate reasons. Find and fix both.
hints: Every subclass constructor's first action must be a call to some superclass constructor: is Square's constructor doing that anywhere, explicitly or implicitly?
Rectangle has no accessible no-argument constructor at all, so Java can't insert one for Square. What does that mean for Square's constructor?
Separately, check the method name Square is trying to override very carefully against Rectangle's method name: Java method names are case-sensitive.
exercises.solutionExplanation: There are two mistakes here. First, Square's constructor tries to assign width and height without ever calling a Rectangle constructor. But every subclass constructor's first statement must be a call to a superclass constructor, and since Rectangle has no accessible no-argument constructor for Java to insert implicitly, this fails to compile with 'constructor Rectangle in class Rectangle cannot be applied to given types'. The fix replaces the direct field assignments with super(side, side), letting Rectangle's own constructor do the initialization. Second, the method is written as Area() (capital A), which does not match Rectangle's area() (lowercase a); @Override catches this: since there's no Rectangle method with that exact signature to override, the annotation itself makes this a compile error rather than letting Area() become an unrelated new method that never overrides anything. Renaming it to area() fixes the mismatch and makes @Override valid.

options: A
B, and A
B
This fails to compile because ref is declared as A but assigned a B.
assessments.explanation: ref is declared as A, but its, run-time object is a B, and overriding dispatches based on that type, so ref.greet() runs B's override, not A's. Inside B's override, super.greet() calls A's version, which returns "A", and B's override concatenates that into "B, and A", which is what gets printed. The “A” option wrongly assumes the declared type determines which override runs. The “B” option ignores that super.greet() contributes to the result. The “This fails to compile because ref…” option is wrong: assigning a subclass object to a superclass-typed reference is legal, and polymorphism depends on it.

assessments.prompt: A junior developer is confused about why their subclass constructor won't compile without a super(...) call, when their superclass 'obviously' has fields that need initializing anyway. Explain the rule around subclass constructors and super(...), and separately explain how overriding differs from overloading in terms of when the actual method to run is decided.
assessments.modelAnswer: Every subclass constructor's very first action, whether you write it explicitly or not, must be a call to some constructor of its superclass. If you don't write a super(...) call yourself, Java automatically inserts a call to the superclass's no-argument constructor as the first line. But that only works if the superclass has an accessible no-argument constructor. If the superclass only defines constructors that take arguments, that automatic insertion has nothing valid to call, and the subclass constructor fails to compile unless you write an explicit super(...) call yourself, matching one of the superclass's constructors. The reason is that a subclass typically inherits fields from its superclass, and those fields need to be properly initialized by the superclass's own constructor logic before the subclass constructor's body does anything that might depend on them being in a valid state. Java guarantees this by making superclass construction unconditionally happen first, all the way up the inheritance chain, before any subclass's own constructor body runs its own statements. Separately, overriding and overloading are resolved completely differently, despite sounding similar. Overloading (multiple methods sharing a name but differing in parameter list) is resolved at compile time, purely from the declared types of the arguments at each call site; the compiler bakes in which specific overload a given call will invoke before the program ever runs. Overriding (a subclass redefining an inherited method with the identical signature) is resolved at run time, based on the, type of the object a method is called on, regardless of how the reference variable pointing at that object happens to be declared. That's why calling a method through a superclass-typed reference that points at a subclass object still runs the subclass's overridden version: the decision is deferred to run time and depends on what the object really is, not on the compile-time type of the variable used to reach it.

assessments.prompt: class Animal { private String name; protected int age; public Animal(String name, int age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; } } class Dog extends Animal { public Dog(String name, int age) { super(name, age); } public void printAge() { System.out.println(age); } public void printName() { System.out.println(name); } } What happens when Dog is compiled?
options: printAge() compiles fine because age is protected, which subclass code can reference directly; printName() fails to compile because name is private in Animal -- every Dog object still carries that field's storage, but Dog's own code cannot refer to it directly by name.
printName() compiles fine because private members automatically become protected once a class is inherited by a subclass.
Both printAge() and printName() compile fine, since Dog inherits both fields from Animal.
Both methods fail to compile, because a subclass can never directly reference any field declared in a superclass.
assessments.explanation: protected grants access to subclasses in addition to the declaring class itself, so Dog's code can reference age, and printAge() compiles fine. private, by contrast, restricts access to the declaring class only. Dog still has the storage for name (every Dog object carries it), but Dog's own code has no direct way to name it, the same as any unrelated outside code would face. The “Both printAge() and printName() compile fine, since…” option overlooks that inheriting a field's storage is different from being able to reference it by name. The “Both methods fail to compile…” option is wrong because protected fields are designed to be accessible from subclasses. The “printName() compiles fine because private members automatically…” option is wrong: access modifiers are fixed at declaration and are never upgraded by the mere fact of being inherited.

assessments.prompt: class Base { public Base(int id) { } } class Derived extends Base { public Derived() { } } What happens when this is compiled?
options: It compiles fine; Java inserts an implicit super() call using a no-argument constructor on Base.
It compiles fine, because Derived's constructor body has no statements of its own, so no superclass constructor call is required at all.
It fails to compile because Base's constructor parameter must share the same name as one used somewhere in Derived's constructor.

It fails to compile, because Java tries to insert an implicit super() call as Derived's first action, but Base has no accessible no-argument constructor for that call to match -- Derived's constructor must instead explicitly call super(someInt).
assessments.explanation: Every subclass constructor's first action, explicit or not, must be a call to some superclass constructor. Derived writes no explicit super(...) call, so Java tries to insert the implicit super(), but Base only defines a constructor that takes an int, so there's no accessible no-argument constructor for that implicit call to match, and compilation fails. The fix would be writing super(someInt) as Derived's first statement. The “It compiles fine; Java inserts an implicit…” option assumes a no-argument constructor exists on Base when it does not. The “It compiles fine, because Derived's constructor body…” option is wrong because an empty constructor body still needs a superclass constructor call; 'first action' applies regardless of whether any other statements follow. The “It fails to compile because Base's constructor…” option describes a rule Java has no version of at all: parameter names never need to match across a super call.

assessments.prompt: class Animal { public void makeSound(String context) { } } class Dog extends Animal { @Override public void makeSound() { } } What happens when Dog is compiled?
options: It fails to compile because a subclass is never allowed to declare a method sharing a name already used in its superclass.
It compiles fine, and makeSound() overrides Animal's makeSound(String) since they share the same name.

It fails to compile, because @Override asserts this method overrides a superclass method, but Animal has no makeSound method with an empty parameter list -- the differing parameter list makes this a distinct, unrelated method rather than an override, and the annotation catches that mismatch.
It compiles fine, silently defining a new overloaded method alongside Animal's, with @Override simply having no effect.
assessments.explanation: Overriding requires an identical signature: same name AND same parameter types. makeSound() and makeSound(String) differ in parameter list, so Dog's method would ordinarily just be a new, unrelated overload rather than an override of Animal's method. Because @Override asserts an overriding intent, the compiler checks for a matching superclass method, finds none with a matching signature, and reports a compile error instead of letting the mismatch through. The “It compiles fine, and makeSound() overrides Animal's…” option is wrong because differing parameter lists never produce an override, regardless of a shared name. The “It compiles fine, silently defining a new…” option describes what would happen without @Override present; the annotation exists to turn that mistake into an error. The “It fails to compile because a subclass…” option is wrong because declaring a same-named method with a different parameter list (an overload) is completely legal on its own; the problem here is the incorrect @Override claim.

concepts.title: Interfaces vs. Abstract Classes
concepts.description: Both interfaces and abstract classes let you declare behavior without fully implementing it, forcing subclasses/implementers to fill in the gaps. An abstract class suits closely related types that share state and partial implementation; an interface describes a capability that unrelated classes can adopt, and a class can implement several.
learningObjectives: Declare an abstract class with a mix of abstract and concrete methods, and explain why an abstract class cannot be instantiated directly with new.
Declare an interface with abstract methods and implement it in an unrelated class, and explain why a class can implement multiple interfaces but extend only one class.
Explain what a default method on an interface is for, and how it differs from an abstract method on that same interface.
Decide, given a design scenario, whether an abstract class or an interface (or both together) is the right tool, based on whether shared state/implementation or a pure capability contract is needed.
Predict and explain a compile error caused by a concrete subclass failing to implement every abstract method it inherits from an abstract superclass or interface.
Explain what happens when two interfaces both provide a default method with the same signature and a class implements both.

sections.heading: Abstract Classes: Partial Implementation
Interfaces: A Pure Capability Contract, Implementable by Any Class
default Methods
Choosing Between Them, and Combining Them
sections.body:
The practical rule of thumb: reach for an **abstract class** when subclasses share state (fields) and you want to write, shared implementation once, at the top, with only specific pieces left open for subclasses to specialize. It models a true 'is-a' hierarchy of closely related types. Reach for an **interface** when you're describing a capability that unrelated classes might adopt independently of any inheritance relationship, especially when a single class plausibly needs several such capabilities at once. The two combine. The JDK does it throughout collections: `List` is the interface callers depend on, and `AbstractList` is an abstract class that implements most of it so you can write your own list by supplying little more than `get` and `size`.

One edge case: if a class implements two interfaces that each provide a *default* method with the exact same signature, Java does not pick one arbitrarily and does not prefer either: it's a compile error (something like 'class X inherits unrelated defaults for greet() from types A and B') unless the class itself overrides that method, providing its own implementation (which may, if it chooses, call `InterfaceA.super.greet()` or `InterfaceB.super.greet()` to pick one, or combine them). If instead the class inherits a method body from its *superclass*, that one wins over any interface default, with no error.

examples.title: Abstract Class With Shared Implementation and One Abstract Method
examples.explanation: totalPay() is written once, in the abstract Employee class, and it's never duplicated in SalesEmployee -- it calls bonus(), which Employee leaves abstract, trusting every concrete subclass to supply an implementation. SalesEmployee only has to implement bonus() (5% of sales, here); it gets totalPay() correctly, for free, and that shared logic would apply identically to any other future Employee subclass (a SalariedManager with a flat bonus, say) without totalPay() itself ever needing to change. Employee could never be instantiated (new Employee("x", 1000.0) would fail to compile, because Employee is abstract and bonus() has no body there.

examples.title: One Class, Two Independent Interface Contracts
examples.explanation: Order implements two completely independent interfaces at once, something it could not do with class inheritance, since Java only permits extending one class. Chargeable and Refundable have no relationship to each other at all; they're two separate capability contracts that happen to both make sense for the same Order class to satisfy. Nothing about implementing Chargeable constrains or interferes with implementing Refundable. Each interface only requires one specific method, and Order is free to implement both however it likes, sharing whatever internal state (total, cancelled) it needs between them. Code elsewhere that only cares about the charging side can be written against the Chargeable type alone, with zero awareness that Order also happens to be Refundable.

examples.title: A default Method Provides a Working Fallback
examples.explanation: ConsoleLogger only ever implements log(), the one genuinely abstract method Logger requires. logError() is never written in ConsoleLogger at all. It's inherited from Logger's default implementation, which itself is built out of a call to log(). Because that call dispatches to whatever concrete log() implementation the object provides (ConsoleLogger's, here), logError() correctly produces 'ERROR: disk full' printed to the console, even though Logger itself has no idea, and doesn't need to know, that console printing is how log() happens. If a different implementer, say FileLogger, wrote its own log() that appended to a file instead, that exact same inherited logError() default would automatically write 'ERROR: ...' to a file instead, with zero changes needed to Logger or to logError() itself.

misconceptions.description: Since both abstract classes and interfaces can declare methods with no body that subclasses must implement, they're basically interchangeable design tools, and the choice between them is mostly a matter of taste.
misconceptions.clarification: A class can extend only one class, abstract or not, but it can implement any number of interfaces. Use an abstract class when closely related subclasses share state (fields) and implementation, with some behavior left open. An interface is the right tool for a capability contract that unrelated classes might adopt independently, especially when a class plausibly needs to satisfy several such contracts simultaneously, which committing to a single abstract-class hierarchy would foreclose. If you pick an abstract class and later need one of its subclasses to extend something else, you face a breaking restructure.

misconceptions.description: A default method on an interface lets that interface store and share state across all the classes that implement it, the same way a field on an abstract class does.
misconceptions.clarification: A default method can only provide a shared method BODY (an implementation that all implementers get for free) it cannot introduce any instance field at all; interfaces still have no per-object storage of their own. A default method's body can only read from and combine the results of other methods (abstract or default) the interface declares. It cannot maintain its own persistent state between calls the way a field on an abstract class naturally does, because there is no interface-level storage for it to live in. If you need shared per-object state, use an abstract class or composition.
misconceptions.fact: A default method can only provide a shared method BODY (an implementation that all implementers get for free) it cannot introduce any instance field at all; interfaces still have no per-object storage of their own.

exercises.prompt: What does this program print, and why?
hints: EmailNotifier never implements send() or sendUrgent() itself: trace where each one comes from in the chain of interface and abstract class.
sendUrgent() is a default method that calls send(message). And that call dispatches to whatever, run-time implementation of send() the object provides, like overriding does.
BaseNotifier's send() uses prefix, which was set via the constructor chain: figure out what prefix holds for this specific EmailNotifier object.
exercises.expectedAnswer: EMAIL: URGENT: server down. sendUrgent (the interface default) calls send("URGENT: server down"), which dispatches to BaseNotifier's implementation, printing prefix ("EMAIL") followed by the message.
exercises.solutionExplanation: n.sendUrgent("server down") runs Notifier's default method, since neither BaseNotifier nor EmailNotifier overrides it. That default builds the string "URGENT: server down" and calls send(...) with it, and that call dispatches based on the run-time type of n, which is an EmailNotifier. EmailNotifier itself has no send() of its own, but it inherits BaseNotifier's implementation, which prints prefix + ": " + message. prefix was set to "EMAIL" via EmailNotifier's constructor calling super("EMAIL"), so the final output is "EMAIL: URGENT: server down".

exercises.prompt: This code is meant to define a Payable interface implemented by an abstract Worker class, with a concrete Contractor subclass. It fails to compile. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Worker implements Payable but is itself declared abstract. Does an abstract class have to implement every method of an interface it declares implements?
Contractor is a concrete (non-abstract) class. Concrete classes CANNOT leave any inherited abstract method (from an interface OR an abstract superclass) unimplemented.
Add a calculatePay() implementation to Contractor, using hourlyRate and hoursWorked to compute the pay.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Worker is allowed to implement Payable without providing calculatePay() itself, because Worker is declared abstract: an abstract class is permitted to leave inherited abstract methods (whether from an interface or from an abstract superclass) unimplemented, deferring the obligation to whichever subclass eventually becomes concrete. Contractor, however, is a plain, concrete class, and a concrete class is never allowed to leave any inherited abstract method unimplemented. Since Contractor extends Worker and never supplies calculatePay(), the compiler correctly rejects it with something like 'Contractor is not abstract and does not override abstract method calculatePay() in Payable'. The fix adds a calculatePay() implementation to Contractor, computing pay from its own hourlyRate and hoursWorked fields.

assessments.prompt: A class needs to share a considerable amount of common state and implemented logic across several closely related subclasses, AND separately needs to be usable anywhere a totally unrelated 'Comparable'-style capability is expected. Which design is most appropriate?
options: This scenario is impossible to model correctly in Java, since a class cannot both extend a class and implement an interface.

Use an abstract class as the shared base for the closely related subclasses (for the shared state and implementation), and have that abstract class also implement the unrelated capability interface -- these are not mutually exclusive.

Use only an abstract class for everything, and have the unrelated capability re-implemented separately by each subclass instead of using an interface, since a Java class that extends an abstract class is not permitted to implement any interfaces as well.
Use only an interface for everything, since interfaces are strictly more flexible than abstract classes.
assessments.explanation: Abstract classes and interfaces are not mutually exclusive tools: a class (including an abstract one) can extend at most one class while implementing any number of interfaces at the same time. Using an abstract class to hold the shared state and implementation for closely related subclasses, while that same abstract class also implements the unrelated capability interface, lets every concrete subclass automatically get both: the shared implementation via inheritance, and the capability contract via the interface it's already implementing. The “Use only an interface for everything, since…” option is wrong because interfaces cannot hold shared instance state the way this scenario requires. The “Use only an abstract class for everything…” option needlessly duplicates the capability's contract across every subclass instead of declaring it once. The “This scenario is impossible to model correctly…” option is wrong: a class can extend a class and implement interfaces at the same time.

assessments.prompt: A teammate asks: 'Why does Java let a class implement multiple interfaces but only extend one class -- isn't that an arbitrary, inconsistent restriction?' Explain why it isn't arbitrary, and give the practical rule of thumb for choosing between an abstract class and an interface.
assessments.modelAnswer: It follows from what each mechanism is allowed to carry. Extending a class inherits implementation and instance state: fields with values, and method bodies that may depend on that state. If Java allowed a class to extend two classes that each defined, say, a field named total with different meanings, or two conflicting implementations of the same method, there would be a, unresolvable ambiguity about which field or which method body the subclass has. This is the classic 'diamond problem,' and rather than inventing an arbitrary tie-breaking rule the way some languages do, Java avoids the situation by disallowing multiple class inheritance. Interfaces, historically, declared no state and no implementation at all, purely method signatures, contracts about what a class can do. So there was never any state or implementation to conflict between two interfaces a class chose to implement; adopting five unrelated capability contracts on one class is perfectly safe because there's nothing shared between them to collide. Java 8's default methods reintroduced a limited form of shared implementation into interfaces, and true to the underlying concern, Java does force a resolution (a compile error) in the one case where two implemented interfaces both provide a default method with the same signature, rather than picking one. As a practical rule of thumb: reach for an abstract class when you want to share state and implementation across a family of closely related types, modeling 'is-a' ancestry with only specific behavior deliberately left open; reach for an interface when you're describing a capability that unrelated classes might adopt independently, especially when a single class plausibly needs to satisfy several such capabilities at once. And remember the two combine freely, since a class extending one abstract class can still implement as many interfaces as it needs.

assessments.prompt: abstract class Shape { public abstract double area(); } Shape s = new Shape(); What happens?
options: This fails to compile only because Shape has no constructor defined -- adding one would make new Shape() legal.
This compiles fine but throws an exception the first time area() is actually called on s.
This compiles fine, creating a Shape object whose area() acts as an empty stub that does nothing when called.

This fails to compile, because Shape is abstract and Java refuses to let it be instantiated directly with new -- there is a real, structural gap (area() has no body anywhere in Shape) that would leave an incomplete object.
assessments.explanation: An abstract class is incomplete by design. It can declare abstract methods with no body at all, and Java enforces, at compile time, that you can never instantiate such a class, because doing so would produce an object with a method that has nowhere to dispatch to. new Shape() is rejected before the program ever runs. The “This compiles fine, creating a Shape object…” and “This compiles fine but throws an exception…” options both assume instantiation is allowed and only differ on when the problem would show up, but the problem is caught immediately, at compile time, not deferred to construction or to calling area(). The “This fails to compile only because Shape…” option is wrong because adding a constructor to Shape would not change its abstractness at all; the restriction comes from the abstract keyword and the unimplemented method, not from the absence of a constructor.

assessments.prompt: interface A { default String greet() { return "A"; } } interface B { default String greet() { return "B"; } } class C implements A, B { } What happens when C is compiled?
options: It fails to compile with an error about inheriting unrelated defaults for greet() from A and B, unless C itself overrides greet() to resolve the conflict explicitly.
It compiles fine, and C's greet() returns "B", since the last interface listed always wins the conflict.
It compiles fine, and C's greet() returns "A", since interfaces are resolved in the order they're listed in implements, and the second default is silently ignored.
It compiles fine, and calling c.greet() throws a runtime exception because Java cannot decide which version to run.
assessments.explanation: When a class implements two interfaces that each supply a default method with the exact same signature, Java does not pick one arbitrarily by listing order or any other implicit rule. It treats the conflict as a compile error, forcing the class author to resolve it by overriding greet() in C (optionally calling A.super.greet() or B.super.greet() to pick one, or combining them). The “It compiles fine, and C's greet() returns "A"…” and “It compiles fine, and C's greet() returns "B"…” options both invent a resolution-by-order rule that Java does not have. The “It compiles fine, and calling c.greet() throws…” option is wrong because the failure happens at compile time, not as a runtime exception: C never successfully compiles in the first place, so it could never be instantiated to call greet() on.
